text: Just like the full backup, you won't find a manual BACKUP DATABASE WITH DIFFERENTIAL statement in this lesson. Azure SQL Database takes differential backups automatically, roughly every 12 to 24 hours. The real question here isn't how to trigger one — it's why this backup type earns its place at all.

A full backup, taken roughly weekly, is Overlook's safety net — but a database that takes real appointments and billing entries every business day can't rely on a once-a-week snapshot alone. The differential keeps the gap between the last full backup and right now small, without the cost of running a full backup constantly. And it's still fully automatic — Azure triggers it, not the DBA.

Remember the rule from Lesson 2: a differential always captures everything changed since the last full backup, never since the last differential. If the full ran Sunday, Monday's differential covers Sunday through Monday, and Wednesday's covers Sunday through Wednesday — growing larger each day until the next full resets it. That's the same logic, now running automatically underneath Overlook's database.

There's no day-by-day differential job history to query the way on-prem msdb would give you — Azure SQL Database doesn't expose that level of detail. What you can confirm is that the overall chain stays healthy: checking earliestRestoreDate again a day later and seeing it's moved forward is real, if indirect, evidence that differential and log backups have kept running. And when you actually restore, Azure assembles the right full-plus-differential-plus-log chain automatically — you never manually pick which differential to use.
That's the differential, confirmed rather than triggered. Next lesson covers the log backup — the one that makes point-in-time recovery actually possible, not just a snapshot of a moment in time.
